_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a2.1: Mishna. Good for bad: one may not apply [the sanctity of] an unblemished non-sacred animal to a bad [blemished] consecrated one, and yet “if he substitutes” etc. Evidently blemished animals effect substitution. And substitution takes effect upon a blemished animal, as it is written: “or bad for good,” which means a blemished non-sacred animal for an unblemished consecrated one.
rashi:a3.1: And which is good for bad: that is to say, which bad consecrated animal effects substitution? One whose consecration preceded its blemish; but if its blemish preceded its consecration, it does not effect substitution. And the Gemara explains what the derivation is.
rashi:a6.1: Gemara. Let the verse write: “He shall neither exchange it, nor substitute it, good for bad, or bad for it”: and it would mean: or a bad one he shall not substitute, neither for a good one nor for a bad one.
rashi:a6.2: Why do I need the latter “for good”? To tell you: good from its beginning, that at the time it was consecrated it was unblemished and afterward a blemish befell it, effects substitution.
rashi:a7.1: He shall not substitute it for bad: and it would imply that it [the consecrated animal] is good.
rashi:a7.2: Or bad: implies: or a bad non-sacred animal he shall not substitute for a good [consecrated] one.
rashi:a8.1: Good for bad: a good non-sacred animal for a bad consecrated one.
rashi:a8.2: Where he improves it: he improves the consecrated property, and he is flogged; good for good, is it even necessary [to state]?
rashi:a9.1: One does not administer punishment on the basis of an a fortiori inference: and therefore the verse was needed, since on account of an a fortiori inference alone we would not flog him when he substitutes good for good.
rashi:a9.2: And Abaye could say to you: This is not punishing on the basis of an inference; rather it merely reveals the matter: where the verse revealed that he is flogged for a good non-sacred animal when he substitutes it for a bad consecrated one, it also revealed that if he substitutes it for a good consecrated one, he is flogged.
rashi:a9.3: For is good less than bad: that is to say, is a good consecrated animal less than a bad consecrated animal? Just as with a bad consecrated animal, when he exchanges it he is flogged, the same is true of a good consecrated animal, as the Merciful One is concerned only that he not exchange anything consecrated.
rashi:a10.1: Exchanging implies [an act] by two people. And there would be no need for “nor substitute it,” for is [substituting for] one’s own less than [for] another’s?
rashi:a11.1: Exchanging is “this goes out and this comes in”: and there, even though he accomplished nothing, since an unblemished consecrated animal does not go out to non-sacred status, he is nevertheless flogged, since he intended to take consecrated property out to non-sacred status.
rashi:a14.1: Mishna. One substitutes one: non-sacred animal.
rashi:a14.2: For two: consecrated animals, and he says: This is in place of these.
rashi:a14.3: And two: non-sacred animals for one consecrated animal: These are in place of this one.
rashi:a14.4: Just as “it” is specific: for it is written “it” [hu].
rashi:a17.1: Gemara. But isn’t the reason of Rabbi Shimon: in our mishna, due to this verse: “Then both it and its substitute”?
rashi:a19.1: And we answer: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: Rabbi Shimon concedes that one substitutes and then substitutes again: another animal for that same first animal that he consecrated, even up to a hundred. [In this reading, Reish Lakish’s statement is the answer to the question just asked.]
rashi:a19.2: What is the reason? Where has the initial sanctity of the first consecration gone? [It remains,] so that he can apply yet another animal to its sanctity, even up to a thousand. Another version, which my teacher said: we read [the text]: “Initially, Rabbi Shimon stated to them from ‘then both it and its substitute,’ and when he saw that the Rabbis expounded ‘an animal for an animal,’ he said to them: From there too I can derive my reason.” And Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish states his own statement, and did not come to answer that objection.
tosafot:a3.1: As it is stated: “He shall neither exchange it, nor substitute it, good for bad, or bad for good”: a good consecrated animal for a bad non-sacred one, or a bad consecrated animal for a good non-sacred one. This is the rule: the first [named] is the consecrated one.
tosafot:a3.2: And which is good for bad? Blemished animals whose consecration preceded their blemish: this is the reverse of the others, for here the first [named] is the one taken [into sanctity, i.e., the non-sacred animal].
tosafot:a6.1: According to Abaye one “good” is superfluous, and according to Rava both are, as the verse could have written: “nor substitute it for bad, or bad for it.” And this is difficult in light of the passage in the second chapter of Bekhorot (14b), which says: Now, a bad consecrated animal for a good non-sacred one, you said [substitution takes effect]; a good consecrated animal for a bad non-sacred one, is it necessary? This implies that “good for bad” is superfluous, to exclude a case where their blemish preceded their consecration, that they are not taken in substitution; and this is neither like Abaye nor like Rava. And it is further difficult: what does it mean, “good for bad, is it necessary”? It was necessary, to say that a bad non-sacred animal is taken for a good consecrated one! And one can say that there it means this: Let the Merciful One write: “nor substitute it, bad for good, or for bad”; why do I need “good for bad,” that is, why do I need “good”? But it does not say that the verse should omit “good for bad” entirely, only “good” alone, and this is like Abaye.
tosafot:a17.1: But isn’t the reason of Rabbi Shimon due to “it”? … Reish Lakish says: Rabbi Shimon concedes that one can effect substitution and then effect substitution again: Rashi explained, according to the first version, that this is an answer, and that is why “an animal for an animal” comes [to teach repeated substitution]. And this is forced, for on the contrary, according to Rabbi Shimon “an animal” implies one and not two; how then does he say that one derives from it that one substitutes and then substitutes again? And in another version Rashi explained that he reads: “Initially, Rabbi Shimon stated to them from ‘then both it and its substitute,’ and when he saw that the Rabbis expounded ‘an animal for an animal,’ he said to them: From there too I can derive my reason”; and Reish Lakish states his own statement and did not come to answer that objection.
gershom:a1.1: From the unblemished: non-sacred animals, upon the blemished consecrated animals.
gershom:a2.1: From the blemished: non-sacred animals, upon unblemished consecrated animals, as it is stated: “He shall neither exchange it, nor substitute it, good for bad, or bad for good.”
gershom:a3.1: And which is good for bad: an unblemished non-sacred animal for a bad consecrated one. From where do we know that a blemished animal is called “bad”? As it is written: “any bad blemish” (Deuteronomy 15:21). That is, where their consecration preceded their blemish, as is explained in the Gemara. [And from unblemished non-sacred animals upon blemished consecrated animals: one might have thought, even where a permanent blemish preceded their consecration; the verse states etc.]
gershom:a4.1: Which is a good non-sacred animal for a bad consecrated one: one whose consecration preceded its blemish.
gershom:a5.1: Gemara. What is the derivation: how is it implied from here [that it speaks of where their consecration preceded their blemish]? From the fact that the verse departed [from its pattern] and said “for good,” which was not needed: let the verse write “good for bad, or bad,” and not say “for good,” since once it says “or bad” that already implies “for good.” So why does it say “for good” again? Rather: good from its beginning effects substitution, that is, where its consecration preceded its blemish, [and not bad from its beginning, that is, where its blemish preceded].
gershom:a6.1: Rava said: You can derive from both instances of “good,” for both are superfluous. [Rather,] one “good” comes [to teach that even] good for good he shall not substitute, [as a person is not permitted to substitute], and one “for good” teaches about good from its beginning etc. [The a fortiori inference: a bad consecrated animal for a good non-sacred one, where he takes out the bad consecrated animal and brings a good non-sacred one in its place, he shall not substitute; good for good, which are equal, where he does not improve it, all the more so is he flogged.]
gershom:a7.1: And Abaye holds that it merely reveals the matter: since he is flogged for this, [he is flogged for that too]. Another version: it is not a logical inference; rather you can derive it of itself, for is good less than bad (as it is written: “He shall not inquire whether it is good or bad,” Leviticus 27:33), where he improves it, so that he should be flogged more than for good for good, where he does not improve it, and not be flogged? Rather, learn from this that for good for good he is also flogged, even though [a prohibition] is not written about it. [The text here is uncertain; an editor’s note proposes a corrected reading along these lines.]
gershom:a8.1: For that of others: the non-sacred animal of others. And “nor substitute it”: with his own non-sacred animal.
gershom:a9.1: If it had written: “He shall not exchange it,” which implies [substituting] for that of others:
gershom:a10.1: I would say that it is for “this should leave and this should enter” that he is flogged: that he takes his fellow’s animal, gives him this one, and takes the other out to non-sacred status.
gershom:a11.1: But one who effects substitution: with his own.
gershom:a12.1: As he has consecrated both of them, I would say he is not flogged: rather, let both be consecrated and let him be exempt. It teaches us that this is not so, but he is flogged.
gershom:a13.1: [And the reason of Rabbi Shimon is due to “an animal,” and not animals etc.:
gershom:a14.1: And Reish Lakish said: Even though Rabbi Shimon said one substitutes only one for one, Rabbi Shimon concedes that one substitutes and then substitutes again with that same consecrated animal, even a hundred, one for one, one after the other. And he derives this reasoning from “an animal for an animal,” and not an animal for many animals together; but for one animal one substitutes and then substitutes again, many animals one after the other, since this too is one for one.
gershom:a15.1: Another version: initially, in the mishna, he answered them from “then both it” etc., and in the baraita, where the Rabbis sought to derive from “an animal for an animal,” he said to them: On the contrary, “an animal for an animal” implies only one for one. And according to this version, Reish Lakish is the beginning of a [new] statement.]
gershom:a16.1: The initial sanctity, where has it gone? For it is written: “Both it and its substitute shall be sacred.”
gershom:a17.1: [According to the one who says one cannot substitute and then substitute again: he designated a guilt offering to atone with it and substituted one animal for it; and the guilt offering became blemished and he desacralized it onto another; and the one onto which he desacralized it was lost, and he brought another guilt offering and achieved atonement with it; and afterward the one that was lost was found and consigned to a burnt offering:
gershom:b1.1: What is the halakha as to whether he can substitute for it: for now there are two bodies and two sanctities. Initially he designated a guilt offering, which is one sanctity and one body, and substituted for it; and it became blemished and he desacralized it onto another, and this one was consigned to a burnt offering, which is another sanctity and another body.
gershom:b2.1: And what is he asking? If two bodies and one sanctity: whether one substitutes and then substitutes again with those two bodies in one sanctity.
gershom:b3.1: Let him ask it without atonement: let him ask thus: he designated a guilt offering to atone with it, and substituted for it, and it became blemished and he desacralized it onto another; what is the halakha as to substituting again with that other one? For that other one is another body in the very same sanctity of a guilt offering. And if he is asking about two sanctities and [one] body, let him ask it without the blemish; let him ask thus: he designated a guilt offering to atone with it, and substituted for it, and the guilt offering was lost, and he achieved atonement with another guilt offering, and afterward the first was found and was consigned to a burnt offering, which is that very same body in another sanctity, since now it is a burnt offering; what is the halakha as to whether he can substitute again with that same body in another sanctity?
gershom:b4.1: And Rabbi Avin, who combines them into one: this is the reason, because he asks one from within another. He is properly saying “if you say”: if you say that with two bodies in one sanctity one does not substitute again, because with that sanctity he already substituted once, and likewise with two sanctities and one body one does not substitute again, since he already substituted with that body, then what of two bodies and two sanctities? For the dilemma involves both the blemish and the atonement; it is reasonably two bodies and two sanctities, as we said above.
gershom:b5.1: Another version: Rabbi Avin raises a dilemma etc. And in this version he does not deal at all with two bodies and two sanctities, but with either two sanctities and one body, or two bodies in one sanctity; for this “he achieved atonement with a guilt offering” is as if [it said] “or he achieved atonement with a guilt offering,” a separate dilemma about two sanctities in one body. Abaye said: Which is he asking etc.
gershom:b6.1: Rabbi Yehoshua said: For a first consecration one adds one-fifth, [but for a second consecration one does not add one-fifth]. That is to say, owners who redeem their consecrated property add one-fifth, as it is written: “And if he that consecrated it will redeem [his house], then he shall add” etc.; but not if they desacralized that consecrated property onto another item, for that other item is taken into consecration, and if the owners wish to redeem that other item, they do not add one-fifth to it, as it says: “he that consecrated it,” and not one who applies [sanctity].
gershom:b7.1: [Rabbi Avin raises a dilemma: He designated a guilt offering etc. Just as he asked above with regard to substitution, whether one substitutes and then substitutes again with one body and two sanctities, or with two bodies and one sanctity, so too he asks with regard to one-fifth.]
gershom:b8.1: Let him ask it without atonement, and let him ask thus: he designated a guilt offering to atone with it, and it became blemished, and he desacralized it onto another and added one-fifth to it, and then this one became blemished and he desacralized it onto another: does he add one-fifth to it again or not? [And if] two sanctities and one body: whether he adds one-fifth for a second consecration.
gershom:b9.1: Let him ask it without the blemish, and let him ask thus: he designated a guilt offering to atone with it, and it was lost, and he achieved atonement with another, and the first was found (which is a burnt offering) [and was consigned to a burnt offering]: this is a second sanctity and another body.
gershom:b10.1: And Rabbi Avin asks one from within another, [he is properly saying “if you say” etc.]. And according to this other version of Rabbi Avin too, he does not deal at all with two bodies and two sanctities etc., like the other version above.
rashi:b1.1: And it became blemished: the first one.
rashi:b1.2: And he desacralized it onto another, and achieved atonement with another guilt offering: after this second guilt offering, onto which he had desacralized the first, was lost, he achieved atonement with another, and afterward this one was found.
rashi:b1.3: And it was consigned to a burnt offering: for a guilt offering whose owner achieved atonement with another stands, without specification, as a communal voluntary burnt offering, that is, from the surplus, as Yehoyada the priest expounded, in the chapter Velad Ḥattat (below, Temurah 23b).
rashi:b1.4: What is the halakha as to whether he can substitute for it: do we say that since it comes by force of the first one, one does not substitute for it, as he already substituted for the first? Or perhaps, since it is another body and another sanctity, for when he substituted for the first it was a guilt offering and this one is a burnt offering, he therefore can substitute?
rashi:b2.1: If he raises a dilemma about two bodies and one sanctity: do we say that since it is another body he can substitute, or perhaps since it is one sanctity he cannot substitute?
rashi:b2.2: If so, let the dilemma be raised without atonement: for this is how he should have phrased it: he designated a guilt offering to atone with it and substituted for it, and the first became blemished and he desacralized it onto another; what is the halakha as to whether he can substitute for this other one? Since it is another body he can substitute; or perhaps, since it comes by force of the first and it is one sanctity, the first being a guilt offering and this one also a guilt offering, he cannot substitute. Why then do I need to say that he achieved atonement with another?
rashi:b3.1: And if two sanctities and one body: is what he is asking, let him ask it without its becoming blemished and his desacralizing it. And this is how he should teach it: he designated a guilt offering and substituted for it, and the first was lost, and he achieved atonement with another guilt offering that he designated from his flock, and the first was found and consigned to a burnt offering, so that it is one body and two sanctities; what is the halakha? Do we say: since it is one body…? For this is what he is uncertain about. And that is why he wonders why [Rabbi Avin] taught two [elements].
rashi:b4.1: One from within another: that is to say, he is saying “if you say,” and it is one dilemma, and this is what he says: he designated a guilt offering and substituted for it, and it became blemished and he desacralized it, so that this is a second body and one sanctity; what is the halakha?
rashi:b4.2: And if you say: here, since it is one sanctity, he cannot substitute, because with that sanctity he already substituted, and he does not substitute with it another time.
rashi:b4.3: Two bodies and two sanctities, what is the halakha? For example, where this second one was lost, he achieved atonement with another, and the second one was consigned to a burnt offering when it was found. What is the halakha? Since it is now a second [body] and another sanctity, he can substitute; or perhaps, in the end it comes by force of the first, and he cannot substitute. In another version, [that of] the Yerushalmi, we read it as two dilemmas: he designated a guilt offering and substituted for it, and it became blemished and he desacralized it onto another; what is the halakha as to whether he can substitute for it? For this is two bodies and one sanctity, and he is uncertain as I explained in the version above. Or where it did not become blemished, but he achieved atonement with another and this one was consigned to a burnt offering when it was found, so that it is two sanctities and one body; what is the halakha as to whether he can substitute? And the explanation is as I explained.
rashi:b7.1: Abaye said: Which is he asking about? Which of them is the essence of his question? If another sanctity in the same body etc., as I explained, that is, one body and two sanctities, let him not ask about its becoming blemished and his desacralizing it etc. And Rabbi Avin asks one from within another, and he is saying “if you say.” And now, according to this version, he is asking nothing about two bodies and two sanctities; rather this is what he says: If you say that one body [another body] with the same sanctity etc. And according to this version, he counts two bodies and one sanctity as one step beyond two sanctities and one body.
rashi:b11.1: But a second consecration does not add one-fifth: and this is a second consecration: for example, where the first became blemished and he desacralized it onto another, this other one is a second consecration; and if it became blemished and he desacralized it, he does not add one-fifth to it. And a substitute too is a second consecration.
rashi:b13.1: He designated a guilt offering to atone with it etc.: as above, so that they are two bodies and two sanctities; what is the halakha?
rashi:b14.1: What is the dilemma he is raising: Rabbi Avin? For it entered our minds that Rabbi Avin’s dilemma is not about two bodies and two sanctities, but that he divided his statement into two matters: the first is two bodies and one sanctity, and the other is “he achieved atonement with another guilt offering,” that is, the first did not become blemished but was lost, and he achieved atonement with another, and this one was found and consigned to a burnt offering, so that it is two sanctities and one body; what is the halakha? Therefore Abaye objects: Which of them is the essence of Rabbi Avin’s dilemma? Let him ask it explicitly, and we will learn the other from it.
rashi:b14.2: If he is raising a dilemma about two bodies and one sanctity, let him raise it without atonement: with another; rather: the first became blemished and he desacralized it and added one-fifth to it (for one-fifth has no relevance to sacrifices of the altar without a blemish, since an unblemished animal does not go out to non-sacred status), and this second one became blemished; what is the halakha? That is to say, do we say that since it is one sanctity he does not add another one-fifth to it, or perhaps since they are two bodies he adds one-fifth to it? And when Rabbi Yehoshua said that a second consecration does not add one-fifth, that is, for example, where one applies [the sanctity of] a blemished animal consecrated for Temple maintenance and desacralized it onto another blemished animal, for this one introduces nothing new. But here, where he applies [the sanctity] onto an unblemished animal from a blemished one, and this one is fit for the altar, do we call it a second consecration? The first was fit only for its monetary value, while this one is fit for the altar, and it is a new sanctity.
rashi:b15.1: If he is raising a dilemma about two sanctities and one body, let him raise it without its becoming blemished: before it was lost; rather: it was lost, and he designated another and achieved atonement with it, and the first was found and consigned to a burnt offering; what is the halakha? Do we say it is a second consecration, since he achieved atonement with another and this one is secondary to it, so that if it becomes blemished and he comes to desacralize it he does not add one-fifth to it? Or perhaps, since they are two sanctities, it is a first consecration in this respect, and he adds one-fifth?
rashi:b16.1: One from within another: that is to say, the latter part of Rabbi Avin’s dilemma rests on the first part of the matter and is not a separate matter; rather he is asking about two bodies and two sanctities.
rashi:b16.2: He is saying “if you say”: “if you say” is what “one from within another” means.
rashi:b16.3: What is the halakha: do we say that since they are two bodies and two sanctities, it is not called a second consecration and he adds one-fifth, since with this sanctity and this body its one-fifth has not been added? Or perhaps, in the end it comes by force of the first, and it is a second consecration with regard to one-fifth? Another version, [that of] the Yerushalmi, like the latter version above of Rabbi Avin’s dilemma concerning substitution: we read it here too, and its explanation follows accordingly.
tosafot:b5.1: Rabbi Avin raises a dilemma according to the one who says etc.: In the books there are two versions, and Rashi explained the second version, [that of] the Yerushalmi. The rule of the matter: where it became blemished and he desacralized it onto another, and he achieved atonement with another guilt offering, meaning, for example, that the first [replacement] was lost and afterward found and consigned to a burnt offering, this is two bodies and two sanctities. Where it became blemished and he desacralized it onto another and he did not achieve atonement with another guilt offering, this is two bodies and one sanctity. Where it did not become blemished, but he achieved atonement with another guilt offering and this one was consigned to a burnt offering, for example, it was lost and found after he achieved atonement with another guilt offering, this is two sanctities and one body. And according to the second version, “and he achieved atonement with another guilt offering” means “or alternatively he achieved atonement,” and they are two dilemmas. And so too with regard to adding one-fifth there are two versions, as here.
